subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

blocks.title: You may encounter any of the following scenarios:

items.text: Focused history: A 24-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual periods and excessive facial hair. Take a focused history and discuss your differential diagnoses.
Counselling: Explain a new diagnosis of PCOS to a woman who is worried about infertility.
Investigation interpretation: Interpret a patient’s hormonal profile and pelvic ultrasound findings.
Clinical examination: Perform an examination of a woman presenting with hirsutism, acne and irregular menstruation.
Management: Discuss treatment options for a woman with PCOS who wishes to conceive.
Metabolic assessment: Explain the relationship between PCOS, insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk.
Amenorrhoea: Assess a woman with absent menstruation and suspected PCOS.

blocks.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine and metabolic disorder characterized by a combination of ovulatory dysfunction, androgen excess and, in some patients, polycystic ovarian morphology.

items.text: Menstrual regularity and ovulation.
Fertility.
Skin and hair growth.
Weight and metabolic health.
Psychological wellbeing and quality of life.

blocks.text: Despite its name, PCOS does not simply mean that a woman has ovarian cysts. The small structures seen on ultrasound are usually numerous developing follicles, not pathological ovarian cysts.

blocks.title: PCOS is multifactorial. Important mechanisms include:

items.text: Androgen excess: Increased ovarian androgen production contributes to hirsutism, acne and scalp hair thinning.
Ovulatory dysfunction: Follicular development and ovulation may be disrupted, causing irregular periods or amenorrhoea.
Insulin resistance: Present in many, but not all, patients. Compensatory hyperinsulinaemia can contribute to increased androgen production and reduced sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG).
Altered hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian signalling: Changes in gonadotropin secretion may contribute, but the LH:FSH ratio is not a reliable diagnostic test.
Genetic and environmental influences: These contribute to variable presentation between patients.

blocks.text: For adults, the commonly used Rotterdam framework requires at least two of three features, after excluding other conditions that can cause similar symptoms:
1. Ovulatory dysfunction
Irregular menstrual cycles, infrequent menstruation or absent ovulation.
2. Clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
Clinical signs such as hirsutism, or biochemical evidence of elevated androgens.
3. Polycystic ovarian morphology
Characteristic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, or an appropriate alternative marker such as serum AMH in adults when the relevant guideline permits its use.

items.text: In adults who have both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism, ultrasound or AMH is not required to establish the diagnosis once relevant alternative causes have been excluded.
AMH should not be used as a stand-alone diagnostic test.

In adolescents, diagnosis requires both persistent ovulatory dysfunction, interpreted in relation to years since menarche, and hyperandrogenism. Ultrasound and AMH are not recommended for diagnosing PCOS in adolescents.
PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion: consider pregnancy, thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia, non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other relevant disorders.

blocks.text: Start professionally:

“Good morning. My name is … I am a medical student/doctor. I understand you have been experiencing changes in your menstrual periods and possibly some skin or hair symptoms. I would like to ask questions about your menstrual health, general health, reproductive plans and any associated symptoms. Some questions may be personal, but they will help me understand your condition. Is that alright?”

items.text: Confirm the patient's identity.
Ensure privacy.
Obtain consent.
Offer a chaperone if an examination may be required.
Use non-judgmental language, particularly when discussing weight, acne, unwanted hair and fertility.

blocks.title: Ask what brought the patient to the clinic. Common presentations include:

items.text: Irregular menstruation.
Amenorrhoea.
Difficulty conceiving.
Excess facial or body hair.
Acne.
Scalp hair thinning.
Weight gain or difficulty managing weight.

blocks.text: Establish the onset, duration, progression and impact on daily life.
This is one of the most important parts of the station.

items.text: At what age did menstruation begin?
When was the first day of the last menstrual period?
How often do periods occur?
How many days does bleeding last?
Has the cycle always been irregular, or is this a recent change?
Have you ever gone several months without a period?
Is the bleeding unusually heavy or prolonged?
Do you experience painful periods?
Have you previously used hormonal medication to regulate your cycle?

blocks.text: In adults, persistent cycles shorter than 21 days, longer than 35 days, or fewer than eight cycles per year may indicate irregular cycles, depending on the clinical context and guideline used.

Clinical significance: Chronic anovulation can result in prolonged exposure of the endometrium to oestrogen without adequate progesterone, increasing the risk of endometrial hyperplasia. The absolute risk of endometrial cancer remains low in most reproductive-age patients, so routine endometrial cancer screening is not recommended solely because a patient has PCOS.
Ask about symptoms of androgen excess.
Hirsutism

items.text: Have you noticed increased hair on your chin, upper lip, chest, abdomen or back?
When did it start?
Is it getting worse?
How frequently do you remove the hair?

blocks.text: Acne

items.text: Do you have persistent acne?
Is it mainly on the face, chest or back?
Has it been difficult to treat?

blocks.text: Scalp hair thinning

items.text: Have you noticed thinning over the crown or widening of your hair parting?

blocks.text: Red flags for another diagnosis

items.text: Has the hair growth developed very rapidly?
Has your voice become deeper?
Have you noticed increased muscle bulk, clitoral enlargement or other signs of virilisation?

blocks.text: Rapid progression or virilisation should prompt evaluation for other causes, including an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour.

items.text: Has your weight changed recently?
Have you found it difficult to maintain or lose weight?
Have you ever been told you have insulin resistance, prediabetes or diabetes?
Do you have high blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol?
Is there a family history of type 2 diabetes or PCOS?
Do you experience excessive thirst or frequent urination?

blocks.text: PCOS can occur in people of any body size. A normal BMI does not exclude the diagnosis, and weight should not be used as the sole explanation for symptoms.

blocks.title: Ask sensitively and without making assumptions about sexual activity or fertility goals:

items.text: Are you currently trying to conceive?
If yes, for how long?
Have you previously been pregnant?
Have you had miscarriages or ectopic pregnancies?
Have you used contraception recently?
Are your periods absent, or are they simply irregular?
Is there any history of pelvic infection, endometriosis or pelvic surgery?
Are there any concerns about sexual function or painful intercourse?

blocks.text: When assessing infertility, remember to consider other factors, including tubal disease and the partner's semen parameters. Do not automatically attribute all difficulty conceiving to PCOS.

items.text: Thyroid disease.
Galactorrhoea or symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia.
Symptoms suggestive of Cushing syndrome, such as easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and broad purple striae.
Medications that may influence weight or androgen levels.
Previous hormonal treatment and response.
Past medical conditions and allergies.

blocks.text: PCOS can affect self-esteem, body image, mood and relationships.

items.text: How have these symptoms affected your confidence?
Have you been feeling persistently low or anxious?
Have concerns about fertility or appearance affected your relationships?
Would you like support with any of these issues?

blocks.text: Screen for depression, anxiety and disordered eating when indicated.
Explain the examination, obtain consent and offer a chaperone. Perform only the relevant examinations and respect the patient's comfort and privacy.

items.text: General appearance and vital signs.
Height, weight and BMI.
Waist circumference where appropriate.
Blood pressure.
Distribution and severity of unwanted terminal hair.
Acne.
Scalp hair thinning.
Acanthosis nigricans, especially around the neck or axillae, as a possible marker of insulin resistance.

blocks.text: Also look for findings that suggest an alternative diagnosis, including thyroid disease or Cushing syndrome.

Hirsutism refers to excess terminal hair in androgen-sensitive areas. A modified Ferriman–Gallwey score can help assess its severity, although scoring thresholds vary by ethnicity and clinical context.
Common areas assessed include the upper lip, chin, chest, upper and lower abdomen, upper and lower back, upper arms and thighs.
Hair removal and individual variation can make the score less reliable, so a patient's report of unwanted hair is also important.

blocks.title: Document the location and severity of:

items.text: Inflammatory or comedonal acne.
Androgen-pattern scalp hair loss.
Acanthosis nigricans.
Hirsutism.

blocks.text: Example report:

“Examination reveals terminal hair growth over the chin and upper lip, with inflammatory acne over the lower face. There is mild acanthosis nigricans around the posterior neck. These findings suggest clinical hyperandrogenism and possible insulin resistance. I would correlate them with the menstrual history and biochemical investigations.”
A pelvic examination is not automatically necessary to diagnose PCOS. It should be performed when indicated by symptoms or the differential diagnosis, with consent and appropriate chaperoning.

items.text: Abdominal masses or tenderness.
Signs of another pelvic disorder.
Pelvic pathology if pain, abnormal bleeding or other symptoms warrant further assessment.

blocks.text: Ovarian enlargement is not a required clinical finding, and ovarian cysts are not synonymous with PCOS.
Rapidly progressive hirsutism, deepening of the voice, clitoromegaly or marked muscular changes require urgent consideration of alternative causes of androgen excess.

items.text: Galactorrhoea: consider hyperprolactinaemia.
Goitre or thyroid signs: consider thyroid dysfunction.
Proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising and broad purple striae: consider Cushing syndrome.
Markedly elevated androgens: investigate for ovarian or adrenal causes, interpreted according to the assay and clinical presentation.

columns: Clues that may distinguish it from PCOS
rows: Pregnancy
Missed period, pregnancy symptoms or positive β-hCG
Hypothyroidism
Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, weight changes
Hyperprolactinaemia
Galactorrhoea, headaches or visual symptoms; may cause amenorrhoea
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Androgen excess; elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Androgen-secreting tumour
Rapid onset or progression, virilisation, markedly abnormal androgen levels
Cushing syndrome
Broad purple striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising and characteristic fat redistribution
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
Low energy availability, intensive exercise, stress or weight loss
Primary ovarian insufficiency
Amenorrhoea, menopausal symptoms and elevated FSH in the appropriate context

blocks.text: The aim is to support the diagnosis, exclude mimics and assess associated metabolic risks.
Perform urine or serum β-hCG in anyone for whom pregnancy is possible, especially with amenorrhoea or irregular periods.
Total and/or free testosterone
Elevated concentrations support biochemical hyperandrogenism. Use reliable assays where possible and interpret results against the laboratory's reference ranges.
SHBG
May be reduced in insulin resistance, increasing the free fraction of testosterone.
TSH
Helps exclude thyroid dysfunction as a cause of menstrual irregularity.
Prolactin
Helps exclude hyperprolactinaemia, especially in amenorrhoea or galactorrhoea.
17-hydroxyprogesterone
Used when excluding non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
FSH and other tests
FSH, oestradiol, DHEAS or additional investigations may be appropriate depending on the clinical presentation and differential diagnosis.
The LH:FSH ratio is not a reliable standalone diagnostic test for PCOS.

items.text: Blood pressure.
Lipid profile.
Glycaemic status.

blocks.text: A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is the most accurate recommended test for assessing glycaemic status in PCOS, regardless of BMI. Fasting glucose or HbA1c may be used when an OGTT is not feasible, recognizing that they can miss some cases of dysglycaemia.
Routine measurement of fasting insulin is generally not recommended for diagnosing insulin resistance in clinical practice.

In adults, ultrasound may demonstrate increased follicle number and/or increased ovarian volume consistent with polycystic ovarian morphology. The specific thresholds depend on ultrasound technology, transducer characteristics and current diagnostic guidance.

items.text: Ultrasound is not required when an adult already has both ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, after excluding alternative causes.
Polycystic ovarian morphology can occur in people who do not have PCOS.
Ultrasound is not recommended to diagnose PCOS in adolescents.
Pelvic ultrasound may still be indicated to investigate other causes of pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding or a suspected mass.

blocks.text: Scenario: A 26-year-old woman has cycles every two to three months, unwanted facial hair and elevated testosterone. TSH and prolactin are normal.

Interpretation: She has ovulatory dysfunction and evidence of hyperandrogenism. If other relevant causes are excluded, she meets two diagnostic criteria for PCOS; an ultrasound is not required to establish the diagnosis.
Management should be individualized according to the patient's main concern: irregular periods, hirsutism, acne, metabolic health or infertility.

blocks.title: At the start of the consultation:

items.text: Explain the diagnosis and address misconceptions.
Identify the patient's priorities and reproductive goals.
Exclude pregnancy where relevant.
Assess blood pressure, glycaemic status and lipids.
Assess for endometrial protection in prolonged amenorrhoea.
Screen for psychological difficulties where indicated.
Agree on a shared management plan.

blocks.text: Lifestyle intervention is beneficial for all patients, regardless of body size.

items.text: Regular physical activity, including aerobic and resistance exercise.
A sustainable, nutritionally balanced diet.
Adequate sleep.
Behavioural strategies that support long-term habits.
Weight management support when appropriate and desired.

blocks.text: Avoid blaming the patient or suggesting that weight loss is a prerequisite for treatment. Improvements in metabolic health can occur without substantial weight loss.
1. Combined oral contraceptive pill
Often used when pregnancy is not desired and the patient wants more predictable bleeding and improvement in acne or hirsutism.
Assess contraindications, including migraine with aura, hypertension, venous thromboembolism risk and other relevant medical conditions.
2. Progestogen therapy

Cyclical or continuous progestogen regimens may be used when combined hormonal contraception is unsuitable or not wanted. They can provide endometrial protection, although the regimen depends on the clinical situation.
3. Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system
Provides contraception and endometrial protection and often reduces bleeding. It may be useful for patients who prefer a long-acting option.
OSCE pearl: A patient with PCOS who has prolonged amenorrhoea should not simply be reassured that absent periods are harmless. Assess pregnancy risk and provide appropriate endometrial protection.

content_groups.group_title: D. Treatment of hirsutism and acne

blocks.text: First-line options

items.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill, when suitable.
Cosmetic hair-removal methods, such as shaving, threading, waxing or laser treatment.
Standard acne treatments selected according to severity.

blocks.text: Additional options

items.text: Antiandrogens such as spironolactone may be considered when symptoms persist despite initial therapy. Effective contraception is essential because of potential fetal risks.
Eflornithine cream may help reduce facial hair growth where available.
Dermatology referral may be appropriate for severe or resistant acne.

blocks.text: Explain that improvement in hair growth usually takes several months, and existing terminal hair may not disappear completely with medication.

Metformin may be considered particularly for metabolic indications, including impaired glucose tolerance or other features of metabolic risk. It can also help some patients with menstrual irregularity.

items.text: Gastrointestinal adverse effects are common initially.
Starting at a low dose and increasing gradually may improve tolerance.
Check renal function when clinically indicated.
It is not primarily a cosmetic treatment for hirsutism.
It is not automatically required for every patient with PCOS.

blocks.text: First determine whether the patient is trying to conceive and assess other potential contributors to infertility.

Letrozole is generally the first-line pharmacological ovulation-induction treatment for anovulatory infertility due to PCOS when there are no other infertility factors. It requires appropriate clinical supervision and pregnancy exclusion before starting a treatment cycle.

items.text: Semen analysis for the partner.
Assessment of tubal patency when indicated.
Review of metabolic health and preconception medications.
Specialist-supervised alternative ovulation-induction treatments if letrozole is unsuitable or unsuccessful.
Assisted reproductive techniques for selected patients who do not conceive with other approaches.

blocks.text: Metformin may have a role in selected patients but is generally less effective than letrozole as a sole ovulation-induction treatment.
Important: Hormonal contraception regulates bleeding and prevents pregnancy while being used; it does not induce ovulation for conception.
Chronic anovulation can increase the risk of endometrial hyperplasia because the endometrium may be exposed to oestrogen without adequate progesterone.

items.text: Appropriate cycle regulation or progestogen therapy.
Prompt evaluation of persistent or unusual abnormal uterine bleeding.
Endometrial assessment when indicated by symptoms and individual risk factors.

blocks.text: Routine endometrial ultrasound screening or biopsy is not recommended solely because a patient has PCOS.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Counselling a patient newly diagnosed with PCOS

blocks.text: A strong OSCE response should explain the condition without frightening the patient.
Model counselling script:

“Your symptoms and test results suggest polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS. This is a hormonal and metabolic condition that can affect how regularly you ovulate, how your periods occur and how your body responds to androgens.

“Despite the name, it does not mean that you have dangerous ovarian cysts. Many women with PCOS have small follicles visible on ultrasound, and some do not require an ultrasound at all to establish the diagnosis.

“PCOS can make conception more difficult because ovulation may be irregular, but it does not mean that you are infertile. Effective fertility treatments are available, and many women with PCOS conceive.

“We should also assess your blood sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure because PCOS can be associated with metabolic problems. Treatment will depend on what matters most to you, whether that is regulating your periods, treating unwanted hair or acne, improving metabolic health or becoming pregnant.
“We can agree on a treatment plan together and review how well it works over time. What concerns you most about this diagnosis?”

rows: “Does PCOS mean I cannot have children?”
No. Some women need help with ovulation, but many conceive naturally or with treatment.
“Are the cysts dangerous?”
The term can be misleading; the follicles seen in PCOS are not the same as dangerous ovarian cysts.
“Will I have to take medication for life?”
Not necessarily. Treatment changes according to symptoms, metabolic health and reproductive goals.
“Is PCOS caused by being overweight?”
No. PCOS can occur at any body size, although excess weight can worsen some metabolic and hormonal features in some patients.
“Will the symptoms disappear permanently?”
Symptoms can often be managed effectively, but PCOS may require ongoing review as health needs change.

blocks.text: “A 25-year-old woman presents with a history of oligomenorrhoea and progressive facial hirsutism. Examination demonstrates terminal hair growth over the chin and upper lip. Her history suggests ovulatory dysfunction and examination suggests clinical hyperandrogenism. I would investigate to exclude pregnancy and other causes of androgen excess, assess metabolic risk, and establish whether she meets diagnostic criteria for PCOS.”

content_groups.group_title: Example B: PCOS with metabolic risk

blocks.text: “A woman with irregular menstrual cycles, hirsutism and a BMI in the obese range has acanthosis nigricans and elevated blood pressure. These findings raise concern for PCOS with associated metabolic risk. I would assess glycaemic status and lipids, evaluate cardiovascular risk, and discuss individualized lifestyle and medical interventions.”

“A woman presents with rapidly progressive hirsutism, deepening of the voice and clitoromegaly. These features are atypical for uncomplicated PCOS and suggest virilisation. I would arrange urgent specialist assessment and investigate for an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal lesion and other causes of severe androgen excess.”

“A woman with infrequent menstruation has been trying to conceive for 18 months. The history suggests possible anovulatory infertility associated with PCOS. I would assess pregnancy status, evaluate other infertility factors, perform appropriate metabolic and hormonal investigations, and discuss referral for fertility management, including letrozole where indicated.”
Q1. What are the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS?
At least two of the following, after exclusion of relevant alternative diagnoses: ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology.
Q2. Is ultrasound compulsory for diagnosis?
No. In an adult with both ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, ultrasound is not required once other causes have been excluded.
Q3. Is the LH:FSH ratio diagnostic?
No. It can be altered in some patients but is not sufficiently reliable to diagnose PCOS.
Q4. What tests should be performed in a woman with suspected PCOS?

Tests are guided by the presentation but may include β-hCG, testosterone, TSH, prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and selected additional investigations. Assess blood pressure, lipids and glycaemic status.
Q5. What is the preferred treatment for anovulatory infertility due to PCOS?
Letrozole is generally the first-line pharmacological ovulation-induction treatment when there are no other infertility factors and treatment is clinically appropriate.
Q6. Why is metformin used?
Primarily for metabolic indications, particularly dysglycaemia and metabolic risk, and sometimes for menstrual irregularity. It is not automatically required for every patient.
Q7. What are the long-term complications?

These may include impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, psychological difficulties, obstructive sleep apnoea in some patients, and increased endometrial hyperplasia risk associated with prolonged untreated anovulation.
Q8. What are the indications for urgent further investigation?
Rapidly progressive androgenic symptoms, virilisation, markedly elevated androgen levels, a suspected mass or symptoms suggesting another endocrine disorder.
Q9. Can a woman with a normal BMI have PCOS?
Yes. PCOS is not restricted to patients with overweight or obesity.
Q10. Is PCOS curable?
There is no single permanent cure, but symptoms and associated risks can often be managed effectively through individualized lifestyle and medical interventions.

items.text: Diagnosing PCOS from ultrasound alone.
Forgetting to exclude pregnancy in amenorrhoea.
Using the LH:FSH ratio as a diagnostic criterion.
Failing to consider thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Missing red flags for androgen-secreting tumours.
Assuming every patient with PCOS is overweight.
Failing to assess blood pressure and glycaemic status.
Giving hormonal contraception to a patient seeking immediate conception without explaining that it prevents pregnancy.
Failing to discuss endometrial protection in prolonged amenorrhoea.
Promising that PCOS inevitably causes infertility.

items.text: R — Reproductive dysfunction
O — Ovarian morphology
T — Testosterone excess or clinical hyperandrogenism

blocks.text: The patient needs two of these three features in adults, after excluding relevant mimics.
PCOS — management priorities

items.text: P — Period regulation and endometrial protection
C — Cardiometabolic risk assessment
O — Ovulation and fertility goals
S — Skin, hair and psychological symptoms

blocks.text: Choose your answers to test your understanding.
1. Which diagnostic approach is correct for an adult with suspected PCOS?
Ultrasound showing follicles alone is sufficient
At least two of three diagnostic features, after excluding other causes
An elevated LH:FSH ratio is essential
All patients must have obesity
2. A woman with PCOS wishes to conceive and has anovulatory infertility without other identified infertility factors. Which drug is generally first-line for ovulation induction?
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Spironolactone
Letrozole
Tranexamic acid
3. Which finding is most concerning for a diagnosis other than uncomplicated PCOS?
Long-standing irregular cycles
Mild acne
Rapid virilisation and deepening of the voice
A family history of PCOS
4. Which statement about the LH:FSH ratio is correct?
It confirms PCOS if above 2:1
It is required by Rotterdam criteria
It is not a reliable standalone diagnostic test
It excludes congenital adrenal hyperplasia
5. Why is endometrial protection important in prolonged anovulation?
To increase ovarian cyst formation
To reduce the risk associated with prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure
To guarantee ovulation
To treat virilisation
